children.name: LM1 Analysis of Dividends and Share Repurchases
Dividends: forms and effects on shareholder wealth and issuing Company’s Financial Ratios
Cash dividends
Regular cash dividends
Many companies choose to distribute cash to their shareholders on a regular schedule. Most companies that pay cash dividends strive to maintain or increase their dividends
Extra or special (irregular) dividends
An extra dividend or special dividend is a dividend paid by a company that does not pay dividends on a regular schedule or a dividend that supplements regular cash dividends with an extra payment
Liquidating dividends
Goes out of business and the net assets of the company (after all liabilities have been paid) are distributed to shareholders
The effect on shareholders’ wealth and financial ratios
Reduces both the value of the company’s assets and the market value of equity (by reducing retained earnings)
No effect on shareholder wealth
Liquidity ratio such as the cash ratio and current ratio decreases
Financial leverage ratios such as debt-to-equity ratio and debt-to-asset ratios increases
Stock Dividends

With a stock dividend (also known as a bonus issue of shares), the company distributes additional shares (typically 2-10% of the shares then outstanding) of its common stock to shareholders instead of cash
The effect on shareholders’ wealth and financial ratios
No effect on shareholders’ wealth, asset and equity
Retained earnings are reduced by the value of stock dividends paid, contributed capital increases by the same amount
The number of shares outstanding increases
Price decreases, EPS decreases, P/E constant
Stock dividends have no effect on liquidity ratios (cash ratios, current ratios) and financial leverage ratios (D/E, D/A)
Stock Splits

If a company announces a two-for-one stock split, each shareholder will be issued an additional share for each share currently owned. Thus, a shareholder will have twice as many shares after the split as before the split.
The effect on shareholders’ wealth and financial ratios
No effect on the market value of the shareholders’ wealth and total shareholders’ equity
The numbers of shares outstanding increases, price decreases, EPS decreases
Have no effect on liquidity ratios and financial ratios
Reverse stock split
A reverse stock split increases the share prices and reduces the number of shares outstanding, with no effect on the market value of a company’s equity or on shareholders’ total cost basis
The effect on shareholders’ wealth and financial ratios
Increase the share price
Reduce the number of shares outstanding
No effect on the market value of the firm’s equity or on shareholders’ total cost basis
Dividend policy and company value: theory
Dividend policy does not matter
under perfect capital market assumptions—a company’s dividend policy should have no impact on its cost of capital or on shareholder wealth
Dividend policy matters: the bird in the hand argument
even under perfect capital markets assumptions, investors prefer a dollar of dividends to a dollar of potential capital gains from reinvesting earnings because they view dividends as less risky
Dividend policy matters: The tax argument
The investors prefer the way that incur lower tax
Dividends are taxed at higher rates than capital gains
Taken to its extreme, this argument would advocate a zero payout ratio
Other theoretical issues
The information content of dividend actions: signaling
信号理论，投资者试图通过股利政策去解读公司的内在情况，投资者的解读会影响股价，通常公司分红是positive signal，说明公司对未来有信心，但另一个角度，分红说明公司已经没有好的投资机会
Agency costs and dividends as a mechanism to control them
代理人问题，探讨股东和管理层之间，以及股东和债券人之间的利益冲突
Factors affecting dividend policy in practice
Investment Opportunities
More profitable investment opportunity, less cash dividend
The Expected Volatility of Future Earnings
The more volatile earnings are, the greater the risk that a given dividend increase may not be covered by earnings in a future time period
Financial Flexibility
When increasing financial flexibility is an important concern, a company may decide to distribute money to shareholders primarily by means of share repurchases rather than regular dividends
Flotation Costs
Flotation costs make it more expensive for companies to raise new equity capital than to use their own internally generated funds
Contractual and Legal Restrictions
Impairment of capital rule: dividend paid < retained earnings
Debt covenants: a response to the agency problems that exist between shareholders and bondholders and are put in place to limit the ability of the shareholders to expropriate wealth from bondholders
Tax Considerations
Double-taxation
Effective tax rate = corporate tax rate + (1 - corporate tax rate) × (individual tax rate)
Split-tax rate system
公司的NI，先分离成R/E和股利两部分，再根据不同的税率进行课税（通常股利的税率低于R/E的税率）
Tax-imputation system
有效税率 = 个人边际税率，即以个人边际税率为基准，公司的所得税在此基础之上多退少补
Dividends or capital gains

All other things being equal, one could expect that the lower an investor’s tax rate on dividends relative to his or her tax rate on capital gains, the stronger the investor’s preference for dividends
Payout policies
Stable Dividend Policy
Regular dividends are paid that generally do not reflect short-term volatility in earnings
Target payout adjustment model
Expected dividend = Last dividend + (Expected earnings×Target payout ratio - Previous dividend) ×Adjustment factor
Constant Dividend Payout Ratio Policy
In this type of policy, a dividend payout ratio decided on by the company is applied to current earnings to calculate the dividend
Global Trends in Payout Policy
相对来说回购比现金股利好，因此美国公司更倾向于回购
在大多数发达市场，长期来看现金股利呈现下降状态，即全球趋势是现金股利越来越少
美国自20世纪80年代初，英国和欧洲大陆自90年代初，参与回购的公司比例呈现上升趋势
Share repurchases
Overview
Share repurchase: a share repurchase is a transaction in which a company buys back its own shares

Treasury shares: shares that have been issued and subsequently repurchased are classified as treasury shares if they may be reissued or canceled shares if they will be retired; in either case, they are not then considered for dividends, voting, or computing earnings per share.
Share repurchase methods
Buy in the open market
在公开市场中回购
Buy back a fixed number of shares at a fixed price
按约固定价值回购固定数量的股票
Dutch auction
荷兰式拍卖，通过对现有股东的要约收购，公司规定了可接受的价格区间
Repurchase by direct negotiation
公司直接与大股东谈判回购其股票
Financial Statement Effects of Repurchases
Using the company’s surplus cash
B/S
Asset and equity decreases
Leverage ratio (D/E) increases
I/S
Earnings yield < interest income and earnings, EPS decreases
Earnings yield > interest income and earnings, EPS increases
Earnings yield = interest income and earnings, EPS constant
Using debt to finance the repurchase
B/S
Asset constant, equity decreases
Leverage (D/E) increases
I/S
Earnings yield < after-tax cost of financing the repurchase, EPS decreases
Earnings yield > after-tax cost of financing the repurchase, EPS increases
Earnings yield = after-tax cost of financing the repurchase, EPS constant
Effects of share repurchase on BVPS
BVPS > market price (repurchase price), BVPS increases
BVPS < market price (repurchase price), BVPS decreases
BVPS = market price (repurchase price), BVPS constant
Valuation Equivalence of Cash Dividends and Share Repurchases: The Baseline
Share repurchases are equivalent to cash dividends of equal amount in their effect on shareholders’ wealth, all other things being equal
The Dividend versus Share Repurchase Decision
Tax advantages：当TD > TCG时，则回购的方式优于现金股利
Share price support/signaling：回购会对股价形成支撑，传递正面信号
Added flexibility：回购股票的灵活性更好
Offsetting dilution from employee stock options：回购可抵消EPS的稀释
Increase financial leverage：回购会增加财务杠杆
Analysis of Dividend Safety
Dividend coverage ratio = net income/dividend paid
FCFE coverage ratio = FCFE/(dividends + share repurchases)
LM2 Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) Considerations in Investment Analysis
Global variations in ownership structures
Dispersed vs. concentrated ownership
Dispersed ownership: many shareholders, none individually able to exercise control
Concentrated ownership: an individual or group (controlling shareholders) can exercise control
Horizontal ownership: companies with mutual business interests have cross-holding share arrangements
Vertical ownership (pyramid ownership): a company/group has controlling interest in two or more holding companies
Conflicts within different ownership structures
Dispersed ownership + dispersed voting power → shareholders lack power to control managers
Concentrated ownership + concentrated voting power → controlling shareholders over managers and minority shareholders
Dispersed ownership + concentrated voting power → principal–principal problem
Concentrated ownership + dispersed voting power → voting caps on large share positions
Types of influential shareholders
Banks
Families
State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs)
Institutional investors
Group companies
Private equity firms
Foreign investors
Managers and board directors
Effects of ownership structure on corporate governance
Director independence
Independent board directors: no material relationship with the company regarding employment, ownership, or remuneration
Percentage of independent directors tends to be higher in dispersed ownership structures
Board structures
One-tier board: single board with executive (internal) and non-executive (external) directors
Two-tier board: supervisory board oversees a management board
Special voting arrangements: improve minority shareholder position / board nomination and election
Corporate governance codes, laws, and listing requirements
Stewardship codes
Evaluating Corporate Governance Policies and Procedures
Board policies and practices
Board of directors structure
Board independence: absence of a minority of independent directors is a negative aspect
Board committees
Board skills and experience
Board composition
Other considerations in board evaluation
Executive remuneration
Transparency of compensation, performance criteria for incentives, linkage with company strategy, pay differential between CEO and average worker
Investors consider whether remuneration policies provide appropriate incentives
Claw-back policy: recover previously paid remuneration if restatements, misconduct, breach of law, or risk-management deficiencies
Shareholder voting rights
Straight voting: one vote for each share owned
Dual-class shares: some shares have more voting power than those available to the general public
Identifying ESG-Related Risks and Opportunities
Materiality and investment horizon
Analysts need to evaluate the materiality of the underlying ESG data
Short-term horizon: longer-term ESG issues may have little near-term valuation impact
Long-term horizon: costly upgrades or regulatory fines may reduce longer-term profitability
Relevant ESG-related factors
When identifying a company’s specific ESG risks and opportunities, determine the relevant factors that affect its industry
Approaches used to identify ESG factors
Proprietary methods: own judgment / firm tools; research companies, industry associations, government organizations
ESG data providers (vendors), such as MSCI or Sustainalytics
Non-profit industry organizations and initiatives
Evaluating ESG-Related Risks and Opportunities
Equity vs. Fixed-Income security analysis
Equity: ESG integration identifies potential opportunities and mitigates downside risk
Fixed-income: ESG integration generally focused on mitigating downside risk
ESG integration
Examples of ESG integration
Example: a coal company faces long-term risk from potential stranded assets
LM3 Cost of Capital: Advanced Topics
Cost of Capital Factors
Top-Down External Factors
Costs of debt and equity are influenced by both top-down and bottom-up factors
Macroeconomic and political: capital availability and market conditions (risk-free rates, credit spreads, ERP)
Legal and regulatory considerations: maturity of the regulatory environment
Company’s tax jurisdiction
Bottom-Up Company Specific Factors
Issuer-specific: revenue and earnings volatility, nature and liquidity of assets, financial leverage, firm-specific risks
Debt features: callability, putability, convertibility affect cost of debt
Equity features: e.g. cumulative dividends affect cost of equity
Top-down, bottom-up, or combination approaches still require assumptions and estimates to derive WACC
Estimating the Cost of Debt
Traded Debt
Affected by type of debt, liquidity of the issue, credit rating, and currency
Calculating cost of traded (especially straight) debt is relatively uncomplicated
Non-Traded debt
Requires approaches such as a synthetic credit rating
Bank Debt
Determining cost requires information for the effective cost of this financing
Leases
Determining cost of leasing requires information for the effective cost of this financing
International Considerations
Estimate using CRPs that reflect economic, political, and exchange rate risk, plus info about financial markets and regulation
The ERP
Historical Approach
Four key decisions: (1) equity index, (2) estimation time period, (3) mean measure, (4) proxy for the risk-free rate
ERP can vary over time; possibility of survivorship bias
Forward-Looking Approach
Survey-based estimates
DDM-based estimates
Estimates derived from macroeconomic models
Limitations: survey sampling/response/behavioral biases (recency, confirmation); constant P/E assumption in DDM; modeling errors in macro estimates
The Cost of Equity
DDMs
Bond Yield Plus Risk Premium Approach
Risk-Based Models
CAPM and factor models such as the Fama–French models
Estimating the Cost of Equity for Private Companies
Expanded CAPM: $r_e = r_f + \beta_{peer}(ERP) + SP + SCRP$
Build-up approach: $r_e = r_f + ERP + SP + IP + SCRP$
International Considerations
Adjust for additional risk using the CRP or the ICAPM
LM4 Corporate Restructuring
Corporate Evolution, Actions, and Motivations
Corporate Life Cycle and Actions
Issuers alter their destiny (as described by the corporate life cycle) by taking restructuring actions
Motivations for Corporate Structural Change
Types of Corporate Restructurings
Investment actions (increase size/scope)
Equity investments, joint ventures, and acquisitions
Often seeking growth, synergies, or undervalued targets
Divestment actions (decrease size/scope)
Sales and spin-offs
Seeking higher growth/profitability or lower risk by shedding divisions and assets
Restructuring actions (scope unchanged)
Cost cutting, balance sheet restructurings, and reorganizations
Aim to improve returns on capital to historical or peer levels
Evaluating Corporate Restructurings
Four phases
Initial evaluation → preliminary valuation → modeling → updating the investment thesis
Entire evaluation generally done only for material restructurings
Initial Evaluation
What is happening? When is it happening? Is it material? Why is it happening?
Materiality = size + fit
Size rule of thumb: large actions > 10% of issuer’s enterprise value (e.g. acquisition consideration > 10% of acquirer’s pre-announcement EV)
Fit: alignment between the action and an analyst’s expectations for the issuer
Preliminary Valuation
Comparable company analysis
Comparable transaction analysis
Premium paid analysis
Modeling and Valuation
Pro Forma Weighted Average Cost of Capital
Model restructurings on financial statements based on situational specifics → pro forma financial statements
WACC determined by weights of capital types and constituent costs of capital
Costs of capital influenced by bottom-up and top-down drivers
Bottom-up drivers: stability, profitability, leverage, and asset specificity
Corporate restructurings affect the cost of capital by affecting these drivers
